items.title: I'm 40. If you’re in your 20s, read this.
items.content_html:
Share

In your 20s, it’s tempting to think your life needs to be planned out.

I quickly learned this was a lie. It appears as though everyone you look at on social media who is also in their 20s has life figured out. That’s bullsh*t. Nobody has their life all figured out.

Not even at 40. Especially at 40.

You think you choose a path and walk down it. That’s not true anymore. Life has gone from a linear progression of events to a total non-linear adventure. Technology has enabled this reality. It creates uncertainty, but it’s also a huge opportunity.

My 20s were full of alcohol, parties, bad decisions, and having no idea what career I would pursue. As soon as I thought I had it all figured out, my life collapsed around me. My mental health got so dark, I didn’t want to live anymore.

But I escaped my 20s. They taught me a lot. I wish I’d known what I know now about being 20-something. Here are the powerful lessons that’ll help you.

1. Pray for hard times

This is the most bizarre lesson I have for you.

When I was 20-something, I wanted an easy life. I felt resentful that I grew up with constant money problems. I felt resentful that the school system rejected me and that I didn’t get to go to college. It left me bitter and twisted. I drank to distract myself.

Now I see hard times differently. 20 years have passed.

The friends who grew up with rich parents, inheritances, or who went to fancy private schools are mostly losers. They became entitled. Most of them got into drugs. They’ve never worked hard. Daddy always comes in to bail them out.

My friends who, like me, had a hard life now have a much easier life at 40. We know the value of hard work. We don’t ask for handouts. We have to earn every opportunity. We’re much more humble. We don’t have a giant pole up our ass.

And we have zero desire to impress people with luxury brands and sports cars.

Things get even more bizarre.

I now crave a hard life. I don’t want things to come easy. I love the pain and brutality of having things not go right. I learn more from failure than from any info product or $100K degree. Hormozi has an interesting perspective here:

Everything is hard. Nothing works the first time. It all feels pointless. That’s when you realize you’re going to have to will it into existence with every ounce of your f*cking soul. And that’s when it starts to happen.

Wanting it to be easy steals away your personal power. It makes you lazy and makes you want to chase passive income that doesn’t exist.

In retrospect, the greatest opportunity I’ve ever been given is a hard life. It makes me appreciate simple things much more. And it makes me more resilient to face hard times, tragedies, and new opportunities where I feel like a fraud.

The same applies to you.

You can either use the hard times as a reason to become a victim, or you can use them as an opportunity. If you do come from a privileged upbringing, then it’s time to do more hard things and reject an easy life.

2. Stop taking advice from people who have a life you don’t want

Here’s what is weird:

Even if you think you want someone’s life, you’re highly likely to only be viewing the highlight reel. Life is an iceberg. The people who seem to be winning are often the most miserable f*cks on the planet.

Just spend time around insanely rich people or high society like I did.

It made me want to vomit. A lot of rich people think they’re god’s gift to humankind and they treat their fellow humans like slaves. Before you model your life on someone else, spend time with them. Pay them for coaching. Join their mastermind. Have coffee with them. Just don’t sit there thinking everyone is winning.

Their career could be great, but that means their marriage is probably trash. Their kids could be perfect, but that means their financial situation could be terrible because they didn’t spend enough time working. The business they built could be cool, but they have zero time for their two sons who never see them and pray to see their daddy.

Nothing is as it seems. Most of the time you should just follow your own path.

3. Having kids doesn’t make you an evil son of a b*tch

I love my two daughters.

Feminists on the internet attack me all the time for being daddy-first. They try to make me feel guilty for having kids or for describing it as blissful. They assume I must never have changed a diaper, because if I did, I’d say that having kids sucks.

Again, they didn’t read the first point of this essay. I love hard things. It’s a f*cking privilege to change both my daughters’ diapers and get covered in piss and poo. Why?

Because many of my friends have tried to have kids and failed.

They’ve gone through years of IVF, or worse, had their unborn baby die 8 months in. This is more common than people think. So yes, having kids is hard, but that’s why it’s an opportunity some people should consider.

There’s zero obligation to have kids.

Everyone’s situation is different. But to insist all fathers are lazy and have it easy is a lie. The modern father like me shares the load.

Don’t rule out kids just because a bunch of raging feminists are mad at men for who knows what. Blindly dismissing an entire gender because you met a few bad men/women is low IQ. Same applies to race.

20-somethings should think carefully about kids.

4. The cool people become losers later in life

No one tells you this.

The cool people in my 20s who drank every day and partied hard are still trying to do that at 40. The bullies in high school were cool and had the hottest girlfriends.

Now some of those morons are still trying to bully me online — except they’re unemployed, single, hating life, and angry. I’m not.

Stop trying to be cool as young as you possibly can.

What’s cool at 40 is very different from what’s cool in high school. Cool at 40 means having freedom, moderate wealth, an I-don’t-give-a-f*ck attitude, not attending an adult daycare, not having other adults tell you what to do, and being yourself.

Implement that way of life as young as possible.

The happiest people at 40 are the ones who got what they wanted out of life. They’re the ones who made a plan, had goals, and went for them.

5. Endless travel is a form of toxic escapism

I’m obsessed with former chef and TV presenter Anthony Bourdain. But there’s a lot I don’t like about him, such as his joking about taking his own life.

He is perhaps the most traveled man to ever live. He had it all. Yet it wasn’t enough.

He took his own life.

Travel writer Cailey Rizzo idolized Bourdain. She mimicked his life. She spent time with him too. She traveled endlessly, too, and came to a harsh realization:

I began to realize that going to different countries wasn’t a solution to a life. I had stopped being able to outrun my problems.

Eventually, life on the road just becomes regular life. Whereas most people escape for adventure, when you’re a travel writer, you start craving an escape to stability. But people keep telling you that you have a dream job.

With my head over the toilet, I came up with a plan to k!ll myself.

It wasn’t about the fruit. It was about the fact that I was living out my dreams and I couldn’t feel anything. Life was meaningless and I saw only one way out. I was going to get a gun. I wasn’t going to leave a note.

You’re better off facing reality.

When I went to different countries I started to notice that they all looked the same. I realized I craved a place that felt like home more than changing countries all the time, looking for a new family or new friends.

Once I found a home and made peace with my family, my desire to travel disappeared. I now travel much less. I love home. I love my neighbors. I love being around friends. This is what the good life secretly looks like.

If you’re 20 then travel. But if you’re doing it to escape, at some point soon, your world is going to come crashing down once you realize it’s not the answer to your problems.

6. “You never know what worse luck your bad luck has saved you from.”

(Cormac McCarthy)

In my early 30s, I was at work one afternoon. A banker from Sydney stopped me in the hallway on the way to lunch. I was pissed. He made me late. He kept me talking for 15 minutes about stupid risk stuff that bored me to tears.

When I walked outside, I saw chaos.

A man drove his car up the sidewalk and killed loads of innocent people. The police shot out his tires right after he ran over a stroller with a newborn baby.

The baby died.

It’s one of Australia’s worst mass murders. Had I gone to lunch on time, wearing my headphones like I always do, I would have been standing right where the car hit people. I’d have died. My bad luck saved me from worse luck.

Bad luck in your 20s is not all bad. It shields you from even worse luck. Perhaps you got caught doing something silly. If you learned the lesson, then that probably stopped you from doing something criminal.

Bad luck is a blessing.

7. One piece of media from your teenage years creates your entire worldview

If you think hard enough, you’ll realize what piece of media that was for you.

For me, the piece of media that changed my life was a DJ set by the artist Axwell. I watched it and it led me to become a DJ. I spent years working in strip clubs and nightclubs chasing that dream. I drank heavily when I got rejected for better gigs.

I really wanted that DJ dream. But in my 20s, I didn’t understand the basics of self-improvement. I was entitled. I thought short-term. I was lazy. I wanted a lucky break. I thought the music I produced as an artist signed to a record label was good (it was terrible). And I wasn’t willing to do any sales or marketing.

The irony is my friend I studied sound engineering with achieved his DJ goal. Still to this day he is one of the most famous DJs globally.

For years, he played in nightclubs and stadiums and resisted the urge to take drugs. He made it nearly 15 years completely clean. Eventually drugs got him.

He’s now addicted to hard drugs.

At 40, I now understand that being a DJ is just being an entertainer for people out of their minds on pills. And that if I did stay a DJ, I would eventually have to take drugs to advance my career and truly understand the audience of drug addicts.

Getting everything you think you want in your 20s is often a nightmare. Not getting what you want is the savior.

8. There are only 3 skills you need to succeed in life

MIT professor Patrick Winston gave a famous lecture every 20-something should watch. He says:

“Your success in life will be determined largely by your ability to speak, your ability to write, and the quality of your ideas, in that order.”

This is even more true in a world of AI. Not all skills are equal. The more human skills now carry a much larger ROI than before. This is why I’m obsessed with writing. It’s how you join the dots between your ideas and refine them.

Those ideas also act as a magnet for the right people.

Writing & public speaking should be mandatory skills to pass high school and college.

9. Don’t get trapped in a fake reality

Writer Jay Alto said this:

“You pity the moth confusing a lamp for the moon,
yet here you are confusing a screen for the world.”

The internet looks like real life. It’s not. Neither is AI.

Since 2020 people mistake their phones for reality. What happens online isn’t everything. The physical world is different. If you spend too much time online, you lose your edge. It’s how people developed ChatGPT brain after 2022.

I kid you not, there are 20-somethings everywhere who can’t think without having ChatGPT help them. They believe thinking is asking ChatGPT instead of asking themselves. They take the opinion of an AI as fact instead of their own experience.

Then they wonder why they get sh*t results.

AI is trained on normie content. On 101 tutorials. You’re getting the same answer as everyone else when you rely on it. Real wisdom comes from failure, rejection, experiments, and interacting with humans.

Be pro-tech for sure, but don’t mistake it for real life.

10. A simple way to tell if your life is heading off a cliff and into darkness

It’s easy in your 20s to think you’re crushing it.

Youth inflates your ego and makes you forget your immaturity, lack of experience, and naivety. Philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche has an excellent way to check yourself before you wreck yourself.

What is the history of every day in your case?

Look at your habits that constitute it: are they the product of innumerable little cowardices and lazinesses, or of your courage and inventive reason?”

If you talk to the average 40 year old, you’ll find (like I have) that their days are made up of innumerable little cowardices and lazinesses. And they’ll do anything they can not to admit it. All you have to do is look at their decisions.

Most of them don’t make decisions.

They see an opportunity, then delay making a decision and end up stuck with indecision. This is cowardice. I know because I practiced this habit for 10 years and it kept me trapped in a banking career like the prisoner of Azkaban.

Do one tiny courageous act every day of your 20s to win back your life one day at a time.

11. Being totally naive is your greatest skill that’ll make you a millionaire

20-somethings are made fun of all the time.

Older people tell them to shut up and listen. That they need to fall in line and listen to a guru’s wisdom. I used to believe this too.

Not anymore.

Earlier in my career, I got to work with the founders of Stripe. They entered the competitive field of banking at a young age. They had no idea about risk, compliance, or banking. My employer ridiculed them for being naive.

The Collison brothers, who founded Stripe, ended up becoming wildly successful. When I heard their story firsthand, I realized that being naive is a superpower.

When you’re too dumb or inexperienced to know any better, you don’t see rules or limitations. “This can’t be done” doesn’t enter your mind. And old, outdated systems don’t apply because you’ve never heard of them.

In my late 20s, something happened to me. I started figuring out social media at an aggressive level. I had no idea what I was doing. I didn’t understand the writing world, publications, or “prose.”

I just published like a psycho.

Not knowing how the writing world worked ended up being my advantage because I helped come up with a new way of doing things.

Being too naive to know any better is how you create something new.

12. Your ability to reinvent yourself many times is the single greatest skill

It’s never too late to reinvent yourself.

This dude, Gunnar Holm, says his dad’s uncle is a great example. Pursued gymnastics and ended up at the Olympics. Began playing golf at 36. Within 2 years he got a handicap of 2. Then quit golf and started making music. In a few short years, he went on to produce Björk’s first album.

People who can reinvent themselves multiple times succeed wildly in life. Because reinvention requires an ability to change. And once you hit 40 like I have, you start to see that most people love the idea of change but aren’t willing to actually change. Sad.

In a world where linear careers are dying because of AI, your ability as a 20-something to constantly reinvent yourself, learn new skills, and change careers is critical.

Being unwilling to change is a death sentence.

13. Modern self-promotion is bullsh*t

In your 20s, you’re taught to self-promote like crazy.

But this advice has a dangerous dark side. You end up falling in love with yourself. You end up writing books, launching podcasts, and posting on social media to serve yourself. And when you do that nobody cares because you’re obsessed with you and your pretty little f*cking legacy.

My friend Justin Welsh said this:

“The people who really matter are too busy teaching someone else. They don’t even have time to care about their own reputation.

They know something the rest of us miss: When you pour yourself into developing others, you become immortal in a way that no amount of self-promotion can ever match.” That’s what I now know at 40.

Be helpful and you’ll never have to promote yourself again. Word of mouth and your results will do the heavy lifting. Your reputation will come from the people you’ve helped, not sleazy “marketing.”

14. Get good with money, or money will control you

Most people in their 20s are controlled by money.

They do things they don’t want to do because they need the money. But when you no longer need the money, you get to decide what things you will do. And you get to say no to a lot more things too.

The fastest way I found to get richer was to lower my desire for bullsh*t luxury. When you don’t need a $500K sports car and a $5M McMansion to feel secure, you don’t need to make as much money. So you hit financial freedom faster.

There are 4 levels to getting good with money:

  • Get the right skills (skills = money)

  • Make plenty of money

  • Learn how to keep money

  • Get good at investing money, so your money makes more money

If you screw up any level of the money game, you struggle by default with money. And money will control you for as long as you’re alive.

15. The need for certainty hijacks every opportunity

There’s no certainty when you’re 20-something.

There’s also zero certainty at 40. Needing certainty is a virus. It stops people from living life and doing things. No one knows if an opportunity will work out. What is certain is that doing nothing will get you nowhere, and likely lead to regrets.

The best paths in life come from embracing uncertainty. They come from knowing if you take action and are committed to figuring it out, then you will. If you only want to say yes if the outcome is certain or guaranteed, life is gonna be a struggle.

What is certain is you will fail and get rejected a lot before you learn anything. What is certain is that winners lose a lot, which is why they win.

Fear of losing leads to never winning.

16. The more pain, the more nostalgia

Your 20s are full of pain.

Ironically, for me, the more painful a situation is the more nostalgia I have. When you’re in the arena it’s not something your mind can easily forget.

The hard days of unloading containers at midnight in blistering hot weather with my brother and no fork lift felt like hell on earth. Now I crave those days.

Same with when I worked in a call center. At the time, I was on minimum wage and a micromanager timed my piss breaks. It felt like prison.

Now I wish I could go back. It’s where I learned all the skills I have now. And it’s where I met some incredible people.

The painful parts of life are the best when you hit 40.

17. Loneliness is a powerful place to spend years of your life

No one wants to be lonely in their 20s.

I found it useful. Loneliness taught me to be friends with myself first. There were several years where I didn’t have a lot of friends. Where I didn’t get invited anywhere. Where women didn’t want to date me because I had zero confidence and was a loser.

I became a hermit. I stayed home on Saturdays. Occasionally, I’d go to the casino in Melbourne and drink by myself or watch a DJ. I liked to read books in the car in darkness. I’d sit on the floor of my bedroom for hours listening to house music.

I knew I was destined for more, but I also knew I needed to work on myself. And the loneliness gave me that opportunity. When there’s nothing but silence, peace, darkness, and you versus you, your life gets real simple.

No 20-something should be afraid of loneliness. It’s a necessary part of life.

Now at 40 it’s the opposite. Because I’ve done things… all the cool kids, influential people, and even celebrities invite me to events or offer me opportunities. What you can’t see on the outside is that the loneliness got me to this place.

18. There is no one ideal lover for you

I’m not a dating coach or John Gottman.

I’m a 40 year old man with two daughters, a bad haircut, and not many skills in the romance department. But I did learn one lesson in my 20s.

The idea of an ideal partner is bullsh*t. You find a person who is good, then you work on yourself and your relationship to make it great.

This will save you a lot of time.

Think about it… two people meet and somehow they have to get into a relationship and become one entity.

Of course, blending two lives together is going to be hard and lots of stuff will go wrong. The romance blossoms when two people are willing to work their way there, not start off as a 10/10 couple.

Here’s how to stay young forever, you gorgeous 20-something

At 40, I now know age is just a number.

Youth is a state of mind. It’s an experience. You can be young forever. At 40, I feel younger than I did at 21. And I have ten times more energy than back then.

A youthful person sees beauty.

And the longer you see beauty, the longer you stay young. The ultimate fountain of youth is learning to see the world as better than it is. To marvel at the simple things and to realize it’s a f*cking miracle you’re alive.

Admittedly, I didn’t always see the world this way. But now that I do, I never want to become a 95 year old grandpa by being pessimistic, cowardly, never taking risks, and pointing out the problem in every situation.

Use your mind to stay young.

P.S.

2026 will be over in a few short weeks (!!!)

So it’s time to ask yourself...

Is your business where you hoped it would be when you started the year?

If not...

You gotta watch this right now.

items.title: I’m convinced 95% of being a high performer is to just do 5 things
items.content_html:
Share

Acting like a high performer is the key to the good life.

High performers get an unfair advantage. They experience the opposite of discrimination. And it makes normies real mad.

Don’t hate the player. Understand the game so you can play, too, and win.

After 12 years of studying high performers daily, I’m convinced 95% of it comes down to 5 things (simple but hard):

1. Be obsessed like a psychopath

Being normal gets ignored.

Passion is lukewarm, forgettable, and common. My neighbor Debbie is passionate about knitting. She goes to Sunday markets every week to sell her creations.

Nobody cares.

She rarely makes even one sale for the entire day. She’s great at knitting but it’s not enough. Her passion doesn’t say much. Contrast that with the plant guy. He’s at the same market. I see him all the time.

He is obsessed with home plants. I’ve never seen anything like it. His car is full of bumper stickers about plants.

He has plants in his backseat, trailer, and even in his hat. He gives talks about plants. He gives some plants away for free. He’s on a committee at the local council to have more plants to be forcefully planted in our suburb.

This guy lives and eats plants. I don’t dare argue with him.

I’m not much of a plant guy. But when he is around, I don’t feel I can ignore his view of the world. It’s infectious. It’s high energy. And he’s not messing around. We will all plant more plants or he will die trying to get us to.

It’s not a nice-to-have. To him, it’s life or death. It’s his mission.

And so people like me, who are good at ignoring highly persuasive people, cannot escape his pull. It’s not his love of plants. It’s his obsession. You just can’t goddamn question it. The outcome of his work is inevitable.

Everyone just gets out of his way. And he’s able to recruit an army of people to help him for free and spread his home plant philosophy. That’s obsession at play.

I’m like this with entrepreneurship. I am obsessed with what the entrepreneurial spirit can do for humanity. It’s all I talk about. My eyes light up. My shoulders go back. My tone of voice changes. Nothing in the world makes more sense to me.

Obsession is unignorable. And everyone can harness it if they choose.

It naturally leads to high performance because it removes most of the need for persuasion. People respond to obsession emotionally, not logically, and they don’t even notice it’s happening. Try it.

2. Have delusional optimism

This is rare.

Mainstream culture has turned most people into a bunch of outraged morons who think a politician is going to fix all their problems and make life fair. The more we consume this high-sugar diet, the more pessimistic we become (by design).

At the same time, they convince us to become victims. This robs us of our personal power. It forces us to rely on someone else (by design) which keeps us trapped. Pessimism sucks away all your energy and stops you from fighting (by design).

With your will to fight being taken away, you’re easier to brainwash. And you can easily be used and abused to fight some culture war.

None of this is a conspiracy theory. It’s reality.

To fight this virus, you don’t just need optimism. No. You need delusional optimism. You gotta be high as a kite on things working out in your favor. You gotta see the AI revolution, not as a threat to your survival, but as just another tool like the internet.

Delusional optimism makes you believe in yourself even when there’s zero evidence.

Delusional optimists bend the world in their favor. They don’t see limitations anymore. Opportunities become abundant. They don’t see their fellow human as a competitor. They even become happy when their so-called enemy wins.

This spirit bleeds into your actions.

When you’re delusionally optimistic about your future, you act differently. You try when you otherwise wouldn’t have. You’re able to silence haters and even your inner critic. You experiment instead of seeing every pathway as a threat to your survival.

Risks and failures look different too. To a pessimist, they feel like death. To a delusional optimist, they feel like free education with some of the best wisdom on the planet. Mindset: I either earn or learn.

With all the downsides from life removed, it’s hard to wake up and be angry at the world, or be any less than grateful for what you have.

Dr Brandon Luu said this:

People who overestimate their chances work harder and persist longer.

Delusional optimism takes logic, math, and statistics and lights them on fire. Your brain looks for reasons it could work when there’s little to no evidence it will.

The world is great at telling you no. But it’s your choice if you choose to listen.

Eventually, if you ignore the noes for long enough, people just think you’re a psychopath and get out of your way.

It’s too hard to fight a delusional optimist. So people don’t. And that’s one of the greatest hidden secrets of the universe. High performers have known it for years. It’s how they outsell without selling.

Delusional optimism is extremely underrated for mental health – Dr Nicholas Fabiano

3. Avoid unserious people

This one will get me a lot of hate.

It’s not designed as a way to discriminate against people or blow up your ego so big, you can’t relate to others. No.

The point is that unserious people are everywhere. That is the bulk of society. And if you spend too much time with them, you become unserious too.

I met a guy yesterday via email. Nice fellow. Aussie like me. We started chatting. Then he said “all that online business stuff is a giant pyramid scheme and scam.” Earlier, he told me he’s been laid off 3 times in 3 years.

He only has $1000 in savings. Been there myself so no judgment. But what struck me as odd is he could convince himself running a business was a scam, but he couldn’t see the hamster wheel he’d been stuck on for 3 years.

It went further. He then told me online education was a scam too. Just another MLM. Silly course bois. In the next breath, he told me he had spent 4 years getting a degree that hasn’t helped him land a single job because everyone has one.

I asked him how much the degree cost.

Over $100K. He took a loan to get it and is still paying the government back with interest. Again, he couldn’t see the clear irony of his situation. This is where he lost me though. I asked him if he was willing to perhaps consider another perspective.

He said no.

Unserious people are like this. They look for solutions but aren’t actually willing to change. They commit to nothing. They stay in indecision. They go from one shiny object to the next until they’re day trading their life savings away on stocks thinking they can beat Wall Street.

On the same day, I had another cat in my DMs trying to build a business in only one hour a week. Again, unserious.

Serious people aren’t hoping to invest one hour a week into a project and become millionaires. I used to try to argue with unserious people. But then I realized it’s like trying to convert a Buddhist to a Christian. It’s possible… but it’s just too hard.

When you stop wasting time with unserious people, it leaves you with more time to spend with serious people.

Guys and gals doing the real work and playing hard games for the sheer of love it. People building habits, systems, and missions without worrying about what anyone thinks.

People playing decade-long games. People investing in themselves. People doing 10,000 reps instead of doing 3 reps, then stopping and asking for an ice cream as a reward for doing 5 mins of work.

High performers are surrounded by other high performers. The code word we all use is “mastermind.” It’s where we congregate. It’s where we go to church. It’s our religion.

Get the f*ck away from unserious people.

They’ll waste your precious time. Life is too short.

4. Take asymmetric risks

There’s this random guy in Australia named Adrian Portelli.

He went from living on the wrong side of town to a billionaire. Originally he tried to run a normal business based on his love of cars.

Nobody cared.

So he turned his car idea into an alleged lottery (currently before regulators). You subscribe to his car lottery and a few times a month a few dumb-dumbs win a car. This idea made him a billionaire. It illustrates where society is at.

Many successful businesses are using different forms of gambling to make money. The Rob-The-Hood app does it with stocks. On the surface, it’s an investing platform. In reality, it’s a way to gamble on stocks and lose your house.

When most people are taking stupid risks and trying to win lotteries, the biggest rebellion is to do the opposite. And that means taking asymmetric risks.

Asymmetric risk is when the potential upside and downside of a decision are very different in size.

The aim is to look for opportunities where the upside is greater than the downside. The greatest investors and entrepreneurs like Warren Buffett, Tony Robbins, Naval Ravikant, and Nassim Taleb all do this.

Their philosophy can be summarized in one sentence:

Take many small bets with big upside, and avoid anything with ruinous downside.

Many people judge risk by asking how likely they are to fail. Asymmetric risk-taking is different. You still see the potential for failure but you focus on how much bigger the upside is. This is how most rich people made their millions. It’s also how high performers navigate their life and careers.

As Chris Lakin says, “Playing it safe isn’t actually safe. You’re trading the chance of winning for the guarantee of nothing.” It’s actually worse than nothing. Playing it safe leads to poverty and deep regrets.

5. Be relentless

Life is just one big game of sales.

And the key to sales isn’t being good at persuading or pitching. No. It’s being relentless with follow-up. Most people are not relentless. They give up at the first sign of friction. The first no. The first rejection. The first “I’ll think about it.”

Being relentless means doing things that don’t scale. Putting in an unreasonable number of reps. My fitness friend Dan Go tweeted 300 times a day while working a personal training gig. Why? He knew the power of being relentless.

He knew if he did enough reps, it’d be inevitable he’d figure out the game.

And he understood attention is the most important form of currency. Once you have enough of it you never need to work a job again. Dan is now a millionaire and quit his job. The same has happened to me.

If your kid had cancer, you’d stop at nothing to save their life.

Why is this way of thinking not the same for every other goal in people’s lives? Well, it can be. You choose.

More reps. More follow up. More believing in yourself. More maniac behavior. More being out of balance. More “you’re crazy, you son of a b*tch.”

Nobody you look up to had snowflake “work-life balance.” All of them were relentless in the pursuit of what they wanted and so, surprise, they got what they wanted. What a f*cking miracle. Who would’ve known.

Closing Thought

Being a high performer isn’t an accident.

A mentor doesn’t bless you on the tits and hand you opportunities. Penguin doesn’t ring you up and say “your life is amazing, can we publish a book on it?” Sony doesn’t offer you a record deal because you’re good at writing songs. Hollywood doesn’t email you because they heard you’re a good actor or worked hard.

No. Being a high performer at its core is being proactive. Instead of “build it and they will come,” we high performers say “I will build it and people will f*cking come because there is no other outcome I’m willing to settle for.”

Maybe it’s woo-woo. Maybe it’s law of attraction. Who cares. It works. I’m proof.

So are many of you (looking at you Tony). The patterns of high performance are obvious if you look hard enough. Follow this manifesto if you want the good life.

P.S.

I’m getting nostalgic at the end of the year.

So I wrapped up 13 of my best clients’ results, added 13 lessons for you, and filmed an absolute banger of a video for you.

items.title: The Epidemic of Asking for Permission
items.content_html:
Share

Nobody likes asking for permission.

It feels like begging. It feels like slavery. When I was in school I was told I had to put my hand up to go take a piss. I never liked the idea of it. Why should I need to ask? I gotta go. If I don’t go, I pee all over the floor, and nobody wants that.

Our entire societal system is organized around asking for permission. It starts with asking to take a piss in school. And it’s by design. It’s how the system removes people’s free will. And it’s bullsh*t.

First, you people-please your way through school. Then you beg a university to let you give them 6-figures in cash and 4 years of your life. Then you beg an employer for a job you’ll probably grow to hate within a few days. Then if you decide to be creative, you beg a record label or book publisher to release your work into the world.

I spent my whole life asking gatekeepers for permission.

It drained the joy from my soul and negatively affected the quality of my creative work. I made music to impress record labels. I published written essays to impress publications and the knob heads at Medium dot com.

And I chose clients for my bank employer based on logos that would get the GMs h0rny. I ended up giving up the permission-seeking game.

Most of us are tired of asking for permission.

The most common phrase ruining people’s lives

I help people build digital businesses. I hear one phrase repeatedly: “I don’t feel like I’m enough of an expert.”

On the surface this is valid. When you dig deeper you realize it’s the result of years of traumatizing permission-seeking in disguise.

Think about it: when are you finally declared an expert? Is it after writing 1, 2 or 10 books? Is it once you have 1K, 200K, or 1M followers? Is it after a degree, an MBA, a PhD, or all three?

Labels are illogical.

They’re designed by the factory-worker economy to put people back in their place. To tell people to “sit the f*ck back down.”

A kid with an AI chatbot can now learn a skill in 14 days and outperform someone with 40 years of ‘experience.’

If you’re not careful, every goal turns into a giant permission slip.

And the gatekeepers are licking their disgusting lips every step of the way. They froth at the mouth at the thought of you on your knees begging them for permission.

Not feeling worthy is crucial for the economy to function

Feeling like you need to ask for permission makes you think you’re not worthy of your goals or dreams.

Most people miss the point.

Not feeling worthy is how the 9-5 job economy works.

People have to give up on their hopes, goals, and dreams and settle for second best. They must accept a salary that keeps them just over broke. If nobody did this, we’d have no employees left. There would be no fake corporate ladder to climb.

A job underpays people because that’s capitalism.

The highest value for your skills is in the open market. But that requires the skills of sales and marketing. Without them, you’re forced to let the employer do sales and marketing for you, but they must underpay you so they can profit from your skills.

In ancient times, most people were entrepreneurs. They ran businesses.

This meant they kept more of the profit and didn’t have to ask for permission as much. But in recent history that changed.

Big corporations convinced people to ask for permission. To outsource their resourcefulness to a corporation for the promise of a safe and steady paycheck.

The promise of a safe and steady paycheck is a lie. Constant layoffs revealed the truth. Most people haven’t woken up yet.

Once you see the permission economy for what it is, one thing becomes obvious: making you feel unworthy of your goals is a critical sales pitch needed to make you give up on them.

Only then can they use and abuse you for someone else’s benefit.

This isn’t a conspiracy theory. It’s just game theory and incentives at play. They run the world. And unless you understand the games you’re playing and the incentives behind them, others will talk you out of your goals too.

Asking for permission feels safe

As an ex-banker, I see the world through a lens of risk.

Asking for permission moves the risk onto someone else. If someone gives you permission to go after your goal, then if it fails, it isn’t your fault. If they don’t give you permission, it allows you to blame the result on a gatekeeper.

Permission-seeking is really just an elaborate form of procrastination.

It sounds like this…

“I’m just not ready yet. Ohhh well. Better study harder. Better wait my turn. One day.”

These are the words of someone who takes their dreams to the grave. Sad. Mentors and gatekeepers make you feel safe, but growth doesn’t come from safety. It seems smart to listen to these people until you understand incentives.

The advice they’re giving you is based on their experience. It’s based on what gives them validation and boosts their ego – not on what is best for you.

Once you see this truth you can’t unsee it.

The hidden trait of high performers

Everyone you admire secretly didn’t ask for permission.

They just did the thing. They assumed they’d figure it out. They took feedback but ignored it and decided to build anyway.

Permission-seeking is based on theory. In theory, everything will work out if you ask for permission and wait your goddamn turn, you piss-ant.

But in reality that doesn’t happen.

High performers don’t wait for anything. They focus on execution because it tells them what they are or aren’t ready for. It reveals the gaps. It’s based on real experience – not what could, should, or might happen.

Waiting for permission just wastes years of your life.

You end up waiting to feel ready when you’re never going to be ready. Because the path of growth is full of stress, overwhelm, and uncertainty. You get none of these things when you ask for permission.

Permission-seeking is a hidden desire for extreme comfort.

It’s where you sit in a pillow-covered bedroom full of doctors and nurses. Nothing can hurt you. They’ll hold your hand every step of the way. You don’t have to worry about anything. They’ve got your back, pal.

See the problem?

This safe fantasy is a p0rno. And you’re the fake p0rnstar.

In reality, life is hard, you play hard games, you don’t know sh*t, and you figure it out yourself. No one is coming to save you. There are no guarantees.

This is the permissionless path you’ve been avoiding. It’s the only path that makes your dream a reality.

The rogue employee who refused to hear “no” ended up selling 100M units

Ken Kutaragi worked at Sony.

He fixed and built electronics, and he wasn’t a boss. One day he watched his daughter play a Nintendo game. He noticed the sound was bad, and he knew he could make it better. The problem was that Sony didn’t care about video games.

His bosses thought games were toys.

Ken did something risky anyway.

He secretly built a sound chip for Nintendo, another company, while working at Sony. His bosses found out. They were furious, and they almost fired him.

Then the head of Sony, Norio Ohga, stepped in. He looked at Ken’s chip and said, “Let him finish.” The chip went inside the Super Nintendo, one of the most popular game consoles ever.

Nintendo liked Ken’s chip so much that it made a new deal with Sony.

Sony would build a machine that could play Super Nintendo games and games on CDs. Sony named it the “Play Station.” In 1991, Sony showed the Play Station to the world at a big event.

The next day, Nintendo got on stage and said it was dropping Sony and working with a different company instead. Sony found out at the same time as everyone else.

It was embarrassing.

The Play Station was dead. Or so everyone thought.

Most people would have quit. Ken didn’t. He kept working on his game machine in secret. A year later, he showed Sony’s leaders what he had built. It played games in 3D. Nobody had seen anything like it.

The head of Sony said yes again. This time, Sony would make its own game console without Nintendo.

In 1994, the PlayStation went on sale, and it sold 100,000 units the first day. It became the first game console in history to sell more than 100 million units. The toy his bosses didn’t want became one of the biggest things Sony ever made.

Ken never asked for permission to start.

He built the thing first. By the time he asked, the answer was obvious. Permission-seekers ask before they build. Ken asked after.

If he asked and got a no, he would have continued to defy them even if it cost him his job. Because he knew if Sony wasn’t going to take his solution someone else would.

The future is the permissionless economy

People who ask for permission are replaceable.

They’re sheep being led off a cliff. They end up being told what to do. They’re controlled. Their ideas are suppressed. They wait for the right time. They hope they get chosen. They treat their life like a lottery ticket.

If they get chosen, they win. If they don’t, well, they don’t think about that.

La, la, la, I can’t hear you, they think.

The permissionless economy operates on one fundamental philosophy: the highest form of intelligence is having high agency, aka getting sh*t done.

To be high agency there’s no way you can do so at speed if you must ask for permission every step of the way. The future is a return to ancient times. Working for big corporations is going out of fashion because the incentives no longer make sense.

Most people will become one-person businesses again. I’m excited by this transition. It feels necessary given the epidemic of asking for permission.

We need to rebuild society around resourcefulness and rewarding those who are high agency. The nanny state is dying. The oversupply of adult babies wasting their lives away asking for permission or getting 4 year degrees that are a commodity is dying too.

Most people still haven’t woken up to the pain of asking for permission.

But the ones who have are quietly building the permissionless economy. It’s time everyone joins the permissionless economy. It’s the solution to the huge meaning crisis and the never-ending cycle of layoffs.

items.title: AI and Irontown
items.content_html:
For our last movie night we watched Princess Mononoke. I remembered loving that movie when I was younger, but watching it as an adult made me once again realize how Miyazaki has a way of expressing diverging sides without picking one. The film shows people, animals and spirits with legitimate and largely incompatible needs, and each faction is further engaged in infighting.

A central arc of the story is Lady Eboshi’s Irontown, which gives people who were largely rejected by society work, protection and dignity. She gives shelter and work to those who have leprosy and to former sex workers. The mine and the weapon factory provide them with a livelihood, but they also destroy the forest around them. The forest’s inhabitants, in particular the boars, response choose war against the humans to defend themselves. Eboshi is not portrayed as a villain. She does real good for the people of Irontown, but also is an arms manufacturer who is destroying the forest around it.

The film anchors around a character called Ashitaka, who has been condemned to death by an unfortunate encounter with a god that was turned into a demon after being fatally wounded by one of Eboshi’s guns. He doesn’t take sides, but he wants to understand and find the truth. Another character is San (whom they call Mononoke), a girl who was raised by wolves and, despite being human, considers herself part of the forest.

This movie’s backdrop is human progress, and it reminded me so much of the challenges we are facing today with AI. AI is useful, empowering and consequential beyond the people who benefit from it. It’s similar to the iron in the story. Irontown gives the outcast purpose and power. There are people today who see themselves in an environment just like that: people who were never let in before and who can now build things that were out of reach. They are wielding AI to their benefit. But there are negative externalities. In Mononoke it’s not just the spirits and animals in the forest who bear the consequences, it’s also other people. Irontown produces guns, and its people are engaged in fights with other humans. There is conflict and power seeking everywhere.

Another, unseen character is the power-hungry emperor, who wants the head of the forest spirit, a god, because he believes it will make him immortal. Eboshi is willing to support that cause, not because she thinks it’s right, but because she is at war with the forest’s gods who are preventing her expansion, so they have a common interest. But there really is no need for anyone to kill the forest spirit, in the same way there is no need for any one country to “win at AI”. What drives it is the fear of what happens if someone else wins first. And the emperor is willing to have a god killed for it. The people who help him with that desire, Eboshi included, don’t understand the chaos it will unleash.

There it also shows the dangers of seeking overwhelming power without comprehension of how to control its consequences. The pursuit of power itself becomes destructive. In the end, the gods die, and what grows back is not the old forest anymore. Irontown is destroyed. Eboshi wants to rebuild it, and to build a better town this time. Ashitaka stays with the people of Irontown after his curse is lifted by the dying forest spirit. San cannot forgive the humans and stays with the wolves. In the end, nothing is truly resolved, but there is a truce that came at great cost.

Ashitaka’s role in the movie is one of a neutral actor. He was wronged both by a spirit turned demon in the forest, who put a curse on him, and, indirectly, by Eboshi, who caused the spirit to turn evil. Yet he harbors no ill will towards either side. He sets out to “see with eyes unclouded by hate,” and in the course of the movie he is seen as an unaligned actor. He helps people on both sides, and stands in their way to prevent further conflict. He doesn’t feel like a pacifist, but he’s the closest to one there is. He’s a truth seeker in a changing world. Because he engages he’s seen as suspicious by both sides, and ends up shot by the people of Irontown when he tries to rescue San.

I use AI every day and find it genuinely empowering. But I also recognize the pain it causes some, and the moral problems it poses. It’s genuine progress for humanity, but it comes at significant cost. And many of those costs will be carried by people who aren’t going to benefit from it.

So it’s no surprise that AI feels like a threat to many today. Communities currently strongly align themselves with one side and fight against the other. The forest spirit did not have to die and the boars did not have to die in a senseless war.

The question is not whether there will be iron, but what kind of Irontown we build with it. I want our conversation about AI to make room for nuance and genuine understanding, for us to look at it and each other with eyes unclouded by hate. We should take advantage of its real benefits, but also recognize the damage it can do, and the choices we still have about what we build and what we’re willing to sacrifice for it. I like to think there is a path for people with differing opinions can find a way to live alongside before losing something we can’t get back.

items.title: I wanted to do everything, so I did nothing.
items.content_html:
Share

The default path is to specialize in one thing.

But people with multiple interests and polymaths like me don’t want to do that. It feels lifeless to us. Social media makes the problem worse.

There are now infinite paths in life you can take. And every day some flogger on Instagram is throwing another one in front of you. These paths used to be invisible. You used to need a mentor or private access. Not anymore.

Every opportunity is public.

And it’s being slammed down your throat like a multi-level marketing pyramid scheme. I struggled with this for years.

I wanted to do everything. I couldn’t decide what.

First, I wanted to be a drummer. Then I wanted to also be a DJ. Then I started businesses on the side with my brother. I ended up giving up my DJ career, which was going perfectly fine. If I’d stuck at it, I have no doubt I would have reached the world stage. I already had a record deal at such a young age.

But I didn’t stick at it.

No. I got distracted. I had no patience. I kept trying to do everything, so I ended up doing nothing. It led to dark depression. I ended up in therapy.

And at one point, I didn’t want to live anymore, as scary as that is to write.

There’s entire decades of my life where I did nothing.

Where nothing changed. Where every day felt the same. Where I just let my mind fantasize about all these options. I can never get those years back. I still have regrets because I now know it was preventable.

This feeling of wanting to do everything isn’t uncommon. It’s been written about many times on Substack (here, here, here, here, and here).

These essays are written from the perspective of being stuck in the middle of this painful situation. I am going to come at it from the other side, having got out of this stuck phase of life, and having picked one thing that I committed to.

Wanting to do everything is often perfectionism in disguise.

I found myself trying to do everything because below the surface I was looking for the one right path. The door I could walk through and never look back so I’d feel like I’d won the lottery. But that’s unrealistic.

There is no perfect opportunity.

You choose an opportunity, then force yourself to make it work. The difference is YOU. In my case, I chose a sh*tty opportunity: writing. It’s full of broke writers, romantic artists, and people who generally live a pretty terrible existence.

They love to scream that someone stole their idea, or that AI is evil and plagiarized their work. They want the act of hitting keys on a keyboard to be god-like and only reserved for blessed souls with the Midas touch who are anointed by King Charles.

My odds of success were low.

The fellow writers I was surrounded by were insufferable and all played the victim. And I could relate because I was a victim for most of my life too. But as bad as the opportunity was, I made it work because I decided that I would make it work.

I took an imperfect opportunity and made it a good one by defying the odds.

By doing things others were unprepared to do. By simply working hard and being relentless every step of the way. I blocked out the noise, ignored the hate, understood the game theory at play, and spent 5+ years figuring it out.

The difference this time is I decided to just pick something to pursue. I took it from a passion and made it an obsession.

This doesn’t mean multiple interests are bad.

There’s a difference. I still kept my multiple interests. I just reframed them. I dedicated most of my time to writing, and then used my leisure time to pursue my other interests. This gave me the best of both worlds.

I could still be a polymath and explore other fields, but as far as the daily work I did, that would be ruthlessly focused on one thing.

I would try to succeed at one thing, instead of multiple things.

The subtlety there is important. Succeeding at multiple things at the same time is highly unlikely. It’s already hard enough to succeed at doing just one thing, let alone five things.

Here’s the distinction that changed everything for me:

Multiple interests are fine. Multiple simultaneous pursuits are the problem. Do one thing at a time, and you’ll still get to do many things in one lifetime.

There’s a dark side to wanting to do everything.

It quickly becomes overwhelming. I found myself chasing dopamine to try and escape. I would endlessly consume content, watch tutorials, go to events, and network.

This numbed my pain and kept me comfortable. It stopped me from creating, which would have forced me to face my situation. This form of escapism is surprisingly common because it produces dopamine in the brain that makes you feel good.

Worst of all…

Chasing dopamine from fake work feels like progress when it’s actually just procrastination.

It got darker for me. As a writer, I didn’t feel like enough of an expert to write about most topics. And I had a bad case of imposter syndrome. “Why would people f*cking listen to me?” I thought a hundred times a day.

This pushed me to want to do other things, and to avoid the act of creation.

Once I realized there is no magic number of years of experience, written words, or reps that suddenly pushes you over the threshold of “congratulations, you’re now qualified,” the resistance disappeared.

I realized people no smarter than me with far less experience were winning with writing, and I could too.

I also noticed people were getting sick of guys with big egos who were 10,000 steps ahead with a particular goal talking down to them and lecturing them. They preferred people like me who were 10 steps ahead.

I always wanted to do everything because I was petrified of making a bad decision.

Now I realize there are no bad decisions. Every decision has upsides and downsides. Every decision has tradeoffs. The perfect path doesn’t exist. We’ve all been sold a f*cking massive lie.

What changed my mind is this: 99% of decisions are reversible.

That means when you’re picking that one thing out of that giant pile called “everything,” it doesn’t matter if you choose the wrong one. You can backtrack. You can start again. You can undo everything and make a new decision.

This took away a lot of my stress.

I began to experiment more. I didn’t make every decision like I’d have to pursue it until death. I could try it, and if I didn’t like the results, I could pivot.

Even better, I could just start down one path, take action, and iterate if I faced issues. This is the Silicon Valley “Lean Startup approach” in one sentence. And it works in life too.

If choosing one thing carried zero downside and was nothing more than a fake tattoo my 3 year old daughter loves to wear (rather than a permanent one), what new decision would you now make?

A wise mentor said this to me:

“You will live multiple lives.”

The reason I got stuck wanting to do everything is I didn’t realize this. I was sold the lie of a 40-year career in banking that I’d retire from at 65, and then I’d die somewhere around 75–85. This immature view of the world died a long time ago.

We’re now in the era of living multiple lives, and having multiple careers. I’ve even noticed a trend of more people being married multiple times in their life.

The “one and done” fantasy is extinct. Thank god.

Once you understand that, it sets your mind free from the prison of deciding on one path, and never being allowed to pursue anything else.

You go from one thing to another because that’s how it’s supposed to be.

Multiple paths produce better outcomes.

No one tells you this. The best life is one where you pursue multiple goals. Why? Because it creates a better life story. Doing one thing for 40 years is a boring story. It’s also a boring life to live yourself.

A few months ago, I realized the moments I feel most nostalgic about are the rejections, failures, wrong turns, and encounters with bad people.

Some people think I’m a good storyteller or writer. I’m not. I’ve just had a lot of experiences, which makes it look like I have a secret skill. I don’t.

I make decisions based on what creates the best story. You can too.

Having a goal helped reduce the noise.

When you have 20 tabs open and 5 things to watch on YouTube, a goal helps you decide what to do. The goal becomes the priority. And a priority creates focus. It determines how you spend time, and what you will work on first when you wake up.

Until I had a real goal, I just roamed the earth mindlessly, jumping at whatever boogeyman or urgent piece of content leapt in front of me.

Now that I’m through that stage, my main goal (mission) automates where my attention goes. In my leisure time, I can drift off down any rabbit hole I want. But outside of that, I limit my consumption and avoid shiny objects.

I found that one of the biggest energy drains was open loops.

Every distraction or piece of content I scrolled past created an open loop. Most of them were never closed, so they lived rent-free in my head.

This limited my mental bandwidth.

With limited mental bandwidth, I couldn’t think straight, and clear thinking is crucial in writing and entrepreneurship. Closing open loops is how I got my energy back. I became aware of open loops and stayed away from them.

One of the first things I did was bookmark creators and publications I liked. This got me out of scrolling social media feeds which would piss away my energy. I also limited my time in group chats so I could focus.

There’s a simple shift in thinking that will help you. It helped me tremendously.

Just begin somewhere, anywhere.

Stop trying to do everything because it’s slowing you down. Choose a path, walk down it, and see where it takes you. Get comfortable knowing you will walk down many different paths.

Choose a path with a goal, explore it, be curious, see what happens, decide you’ll make it a great experience, and iterate if something goes wrong.

The biggest mistake isn’t making the wrong decision about which path to choose. The biggest mistake is never choosing at all because that leads you to do nothing. And doing nothing leads you to terrible regrets either now or later.

You’ll feel like you wasted your youth. And the truth is you’ll never be as young as you are right now, so you may as well go for it.

Doing nothing is the definition of wasting your life. Take the first step and walk down a path. That’s how you get unstuck right now.

P.S.

A little reminder...

Most people are missing this era’s biggest opportunity in digital business.

Why?

Because they’re too unfocused (for all the reasons we just talked about)

Those of us who just ACT and COMMIT?

Well, good things happen

items.title: The Highest Forms of Intelligence (None of Them Look Smart)
items.content_html:
Share

I’m embarrassed to say I never went to college.

I left high school 2 years before I was supposed to finish. I later tried to go back to school at 19 years old. The school principal thought I might have been a p3dophile and just wanted to return to hit on young girls (no joke).

I convinced them I wasn’t a predator. They let me back into school. And I graduated high school with terrible grades, right before I turned 20. Because of this, I’ve always had an insecurity around my own intelligence.

I’ve always secretly been annoyed at my lower than normal IQ. I thought it was a weakness. I even thought about going to university to get an MBA just to signal status / look smart and prove to the intellectuals that I can be at their level.

Over the last year my understanding of intelligence has totally changed. And I’m not the only one who got it wrong. Most people misunderstand what true intelligence is.

What intelligence isn’t:

  • High IQ

  • Sounding smart

  • Lots of credentials

  • A sense of superiority

  • Entitlement/privilege

  • Years of experience

  • Job titles

Here are the highest forms of intelligence I’ve seen firsthand in people who actually do sh*t and perform at the top of their field. (Warning: some are controversial.) Everything else is f*cking noise from fake-smart people.

1. Obsession

Many people are intelligent. They are smart on paper. They are book smart. But because they’re not obsessed, they don’t put all their theory and frameworks into practice. That leads to massive failure.

Obsession can’t be taught. It’s a way of life.

The word obsession secretly appears in every biography of every successful person in history. Just analyze David Senra’s Founders podcast episodes and you’ll repeatedly see the word obsession.

Passion isn’t enough. It’s lukewarm. It’s forgettable. It leads to a hobbyist mindset.

And it lacks intensity. So it doesn’t create outcomes. Many people get stuck for decades with their lukewarm passion and can’t understand what their roadblock is. I see it daily with people I interact with on Substack.

For years, I messed around being passionate. I was halfway into my banking career and halfway out. I wasn’t serious about romance either. I just wanted endless girlfriends. I dabbled with businesses too. One minute vending machines, next minute passive income digital products.

The moment I discovered obsession, everything changed.

It felt like I’d found god mode. Like nothing could stop me. Like there was no competition. This moment happened when a fellow writer got on a Zoom call with me. He spoke about my writing obsession.

Until he said I was obsessed with writing, I never thought about it that way. I realized he was right. My obsession with content wasn’t normal. It was crazy. It was relentless. It was high intensity and high reps. He said that was the secret to my success.

I’d never thought about it like that. He was right.

Nobody could match me on social media because I was obsessed like a psychopath. I had a level of intensity that scared people, and I didn’t sit there like an adult baby complaining about algorithms or low likes.

Obsession helps you transcend normality into a different layer of consciousness.

The intangibles it creates are hard to quantify, but at a base level it created better outcomes, intense aura, authority, and a perception of being a leader.

What Naval Ravikant says applies to obsession perfectly:

The only real test of intelligence is if you get what you want out of life.

2. Game theory

Smart people lose in life because they don’t understand the game they’re playing.

I did this too. I played the game without knowing the rules and got frustrated when things didn’t go my way. I tried to climb the corporate ladder the “right” way: keeping my head down, waiting for promotions, and racking up years of experience.

It didn’t work. People less smart than me rose faster. How?

They kissed ass and built a network.

They got opportunities because of who they knew, not because of skill. Game theory teaches you to understand the incentives of a game before you play it.

If you don’t, you’re guaranteed to lose.

So, when I learned this, I spent time having coffees with people and building my network. I got on the radar of people who could give me promotions.

Within a year, I went from a minimum-wage call center worker to being at Director level and helping Silicon Valley tech companies enter the Australian market.

This was a job everyone wanted.

Still to this day I look back and realize what an incredible opportunity it was. And I got it because of who I knew, not what I knew. That’s the power of game theory.

It goes deeper.

Once you truly understand everything in life is a game – careers, relationships, money, health – then you either become obsessed with the prize you get from winning the game, or the love of playing the game.

  • Amateurs are obsessed with prizes. They want the passive income so they can sit on the beach and jerk off to Onlyf*ns.

  • Masters fall in love with playing. They live to keep playing. They never want the game to end.

This ties back to obsession. Obsessed people love the game. You can be Novak Djokovic and win 102 elite tennis tournaments and still not want to quit. Because it’s not about winning. It’s about the love of the game.

A hater asked me the other day why I keep doing what I do online if I’m already a millionaire. I thought about it, then replied: “Money allows me to keep playing the game and to play the game at higher levels.”

You must practice the principles of game theory to be truly intelligent. Only a lab rat chases the cheese endlessly through a maze to get endless dopamine hits.

3. Pattern recognition

Every goal you want in life has a pattern.

True high intelligence isn’t going it alone with trial and error and relying on luck or hope. It’s not living a life of randomness either. No. It’s noticing the patterns and studying them.

This only works if you do an extreme number of reps. Otherwise, you’re drawing conclusions from a tiny data set and thinking you’re a freaking genius. Notice how I didn’t say watching passively on the sidelines or consuming more information?

Now you see why most people don’t see the patterns hiding in plain sight.

They never do enough (or any) reps to see the patterns. Or they do the reps, but they don’t proactively study the patterns the way an NFL coach studies game tapes after a big loss.

Seeing patterns isn’t enough, though.

True high intelligence is seeing the link between the patterns. Genius level is seeing patterns between different industries or totally unrelated ideas.

The best way to join the dots is by writing. That’s why writing a weekly newsletter is one of the best things you can ever do in life. It forces you to see patterns, and those patterns reveal deep wisdom.

4. Delusional optimism

Some days I can’t even log into social media.

There’s so much pessimism in the world. People have never been more fearful about problems that have existed for years.

And now AI has made people hallucinate. They think AI is going to replace everything because clever tech bros made them believe that. This is why having delusional optimism is an act of rebellion in modern culture.

True intelligence is understanding just how irrational the human mind is. It’s understanding the basics of human psychology, so your ape brain doesn’t scare you out of every good opportunity by mistaking a tiny insect for a lion.

Delusional optimism goes a step further. It’s optimism combined with self-belief, and I’ll-f*ck-around-and-figure-it-out energy.

Often there is no reason to be this delusional.

You just decide to do it because the alternative is low performance and psychological bankruptcy on every level (including financial).

When you’re not delusionally optimistic, you’ll give up easily. You’ll chase short-term goals. You’ll lack patience. And that means you won’t get what you want out of life which, as Naval Ravikant says, is low intelligence.

Doctor Brandon Luu shared a medical study that backs this up:

Delusional optimism is a secret to success.

People who overestimate their chances work harder and persist longer.

Even against the odds, that extra persistence turns failures into wins.

The willingness to back yourself and be delusionally optimistic produces outsized outcomes. And that’s the only intelligence that counts.

5. Admitting you’re wrong

Highly intelligent people are okay with looking stupid for years (even decades) to get what they want. And most of all, they’re not afraid to admit when they’re wrong.

In 1982, a c0cky investor named Ray Dalio was sure he’d figured out the future. He did what many financial gurus do and he pretended to be a fortune-teller or prophet.

Ray believed a debt crisis was about to wreck the global economy. And he didn’t just believe it quietly. He went on national TV. He wrote columns about it. Congress even asked him to testify.

Then Mexico defaulted on its debt, and for a moment Ray looked like a f*cking genius.

But the next great depression never came. The American Federal Reserve eased up. The stock market took off and kept going up. Ray was wrong. And everyone had watched him be wrong: on TV, in the papers, and in the Congressional record.

The consequences came fast. Real fast.

He lost his clients’ money, then his own. He laid off every employee at Bridgewater until it was just him alone in an office. He had to let his team go one by one until only he and one employee, Coleman, were left. Then Coleman had to go too.

He was so broke he had to borrow $4,000 from his dad to pay the family bills.

Most people would’ve protected their ego at this point. They’d say the timing was off, or the Fed got lucky, or they were “early, not wrong.”

Ray didn’t do that.

Years later he summed it up in 5 words: “I couldn’t have been more wrong.”

Then he asked a better question than “how do I prove I was right?” He asked: “How do I know I’m right?”

That question changed everything.

He stopped trying to be certain & started building a system that could survive him being wrong. He looked for the smartest people who disagreed with him & had them pick his ideas apart. He wrote down every painful mistake so he wouldn’t repeat it.

That system became Bridgewater, which grew into the largest hedge fund in the world.

Asked what he’d tell his younger self, Ray didn’t say “be smarter.” He said: “Why are you so stupidly arrogant!?!”

The smartest person in the room is rarely the one who’s always right. It’s the one who can say “I was wrong” out loud, in public, and then go fix it.

Your ego wants to be right. Your intelligence wants to get it right. They aren’t the same thing.

True intelligence is extreme humility. It’s the ability to be wrong and iterate fast. That’s how you produce uncommon outcomes and get what you want out of life. I pity the fool who thinks he is always right.

They are their own worst enemy. My old toxic micromanaging boss was like this. He thought his sh*t didn’t stink. He worshipped his own awesomeness. And now it’s left him unemployed.

Because people want to be led. But they don’t want to follow a knob head with a big ego who thinks they’re flawless. This is also why the influencer movement on social media died. We’re all sick of fake gurus and their polished success stories full of hidden lies and exaggeration.

We’re now in the AI era of authenticity. Time for everyone to show wins and losses, or risk being fake-smart.

Final Thought

Society has lost the plot.

We’re not worshipping true forms of intelligence. We’re being led by people who don’t get what they want out of life, who are trying to dictate how we should think and act.

It’s time you think for yourself. It’s time for you to use these odd forms of intelligence to produce uncommon results. Because people can argue about how smart you are, but they can’t argue with intelligence that produces real results.

People no longer respect scholarship or papers full of theory. People respect outcomes that produce change, heal pain, and make the world better. The good news it’s never been easier to join this movement.

You just have to focus on the right forms of intelligence.

P.S.

I’m sick and tired of all the “guru speak” everyone seems to be gobbling up today.

No, you CANNOT spin up a faceless Instagram account, have Claude write the posts, and casually bank $500K in a month.

Doesn’t work that way.

But there IS a reliable way to earn consistent revenue online.

Takes a little guts, and it’s definitely NOT for cowards.

I spill the details in today’s new video. Watch it now
